title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Economics (9708)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Economics 9708 syllabus for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (version 2, published December 2025)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and sub-topic headings (1 Basic economic ideas and resource allocation ... 11.6 Globalisation) are transcribed with their printed numbers; objective codes are the printed learning-outcome references (topic, sub-topic, outcome number, e.g. 2.2.3), paraphrased in our own words. Where the printed numbering runs several outcomes together (4.1.2-4.1.4, 7.4, 7.6, 7.8, 9.1) the codes are sequential and ours. The two sections (AS and A), the stage labels and the Examination skills section (codes SK1.1 ...) are ours. No syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-08): the official PDF 'Cambridge International AS & A Level Economics 9708 syllabus for 2026, 2027 and 2028', version 2, published December 2025, read through a pdftotext rendering. Exams are in the June and November series (March for India). Check headings and objective codes against the PDF.

Routes as printed: AS Level only (Papers 1 and 2 in one series; grades a-e); A Level staged over two years (AS in year 1, carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4); A Level in one series (all four papers; grades A*-E). Route A here covers both A Level routes.

Weightings: Paper 1 33% of AS and 17% of A Level; Paper 2 67% and 33%; Paper 3 17% of A Level; Paper 4 33% of A Level. weightingPercent records the A Level share; the AS shares are in each paper's description. Assessment objectives: AO1 knowledge and understanding 35% of AS and 40% of A Level (Paper 1 47%, Paper 2 33%, Paper 3 47%, Paper 4 37%); AO2 analysis 40% and 35%; AO3 evaluation 25% of both (Paper 1 13%, Paper 2 30%, Paper 3 13%, Paper 4 30%) as read from a table whose numbers came out partly scrambled; check them.

Question forms: Papers 1 and 3 are 30 multiple-choice questions of 1 mark each. Paper 2 (60 marks, 2 hours): Section A one compulsory data-response question of 20 marks with approximately six parts; Section B one essay from two (microeconomics) and Section C one from two (macroeconomics), each essay 20 marks in two parts. Paper 4 (60 marks, 2 hours): Section A one compulsory data-response question of 20 marks with four parts; Sections B and C as in Paper 2 but the essays are unstructured, with no parts. Sections B and C are marked with a levels-based mark scheme. The sizes of the parts are not printed; our practice convention (essay parts 8 and 12 marks in Paper 2) must be checked against specimen and recent papers.

Calculators may be used in all papers; formulae are not given in the question papers. AS content is assumed knowledge for Papers 3 and 4 and is not their direct focus. The syllabus limits AS depth in places (the multiplier, marginal and average propensities and policy conflicts are not required at AS; calculation of the Gini coefficient is not required at AS; net present value is not required).

Stage labels: a concept is labelled with the stage of the node that covers it. Several AS-labelled lessons carry an A Level extension taught in the same lesson (market failure 7.3.5-7.3.6, the Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve 11.2.5, the full list of intervention measures 8.1.1 in separate lessons, policies to reduce inflation 9.4.6, expenditure-switching and expenditure-reducing policies 11.1.2-11.1.3); the node descriptions say where. Node 10.1 (A Level policy objectives) has no concept of its own: its content is taught in the lesson covered at 5.1.

This syllabus is for examination in 2026, 2027 and 2028; the document says textbooks endorsed for examination from 2023 remain suitable, so it follows a 2023-2025 syllabus (not in the repository). Candidates from 2029 will follow a later syllabus (not in the repository); check the Cambridge website for it and add a new version file.
overview: Cambridge International AS & A Level Economics (9708) is a two-stage course. The AS Level content (topics 1-6) covers basic economic ideas and resource allocation, the price system (demand, supply, elasticity, equilibrium, surplus), government microeconomic intervention, the macroeconomy (national income, the circular flow, AD/AS, growth, unemployment, price stability), macroeconomic policy (fiscal, monetary and supply-side) and international trade, protectionism, the current account and exchange rates. The A Level content (topics 7-11) adds utility and indifference curves, efficiency and market failure, costs, revenue and market structures, the growth and objectives of firms, policies to correct market failure, equity and labour markets, the multiplier, growth and sustainability, unemployment, money and banking, policy interrelationships and effectiveness, the balance of payments and exchange rate systems, economic development, aid, multinational companies and globalisation.
assessmentOverview: AS Level candidates take Paper 1 Multiple Choice (1 hour, 30 marks) and Paper 2 Data Response and Essays (2 hours, 60 marks). A Level candidates also take Paper 3 A Level Multiple Choice (1 hour 15 minutes, 30 marks) and Paper 4 A Level Data Response and Essays (2 hours, 60 marks), either in the same series or in a later one, carrying forward their AS result.

components.name: Paper 1: AS Level Multiple Choice
components.description: 30 multiple-choice questions on the AS Level content (AO1, AO2 and AO3). 33% of AS Level, 17% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 2: AS Level Data Response and Essays
components.description: Section A one compulsory data-response question (20 marks, approximately six parts); Section B one essay from two on microeconomics and Section C one essay from two on macroeconomics (20 marks each, two parts each). AS Level content. 67% of AS Level, 33% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 3: A Level Multiple Choice
components.description: 30 multiple-choice questions on the A Level content; AS Level content assumed (AO1, AO2 and AO3). 17% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 4: A Level Data Response and Essays
components.description: Section A one compulsory data-response question (20 marks, four parts); Section B one essay from two on microeconomics and Section C one essay from two on macroeconomics (20 marks each, unstructured with no parts). A Level content; AS Level content assumed. 33% of A Level.

routes.name: AS Level
routes.description: Papers 1 and 2 (grades a-e). Also the first year of the staged A Level route.

routes.name: A Level
routes.description: All four papers, in one series or staged (AS Level carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4) (grades A*-E).

topics.name: AS Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 1-6: studied by all candidates; examined in Papers 1 and 2 and assumed knowledge for Papers 3 and 4.

children.name: Basic economic ideas and resource allocation (AS Level)

objectives.text: Explain the fundamental economic problem of scarcity.
Explain the need to make choices at the level of individuals, firms and governments.
Define opportunity cost and show how it arises from choices.
Explain the basic questions of resource allocation: what, how and for whom to produce.
Describe economics as a social science.
Distinguish positive from normative statements (facts from value judgements).
Explain the meaning of ceteris paribus.
Explain the importance of the time period: short run, long run and very long run.

children.name: Factors of production
children.description: Rewards to the factors (1.3.3) are taught in the distribution lesson covered here; specialisation and the entrepreneur (1.3.4-1.3.5) in one lesson.

objectives.text: Define the factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Distinguish human capital from physical capital.
Identify the rewards to the factors of production.
Explain the division of labour and specialisation.
Explain the role of the entrepreneur in contemporary economies: bearing risk and organising the other factors.

children.name: Resource allocation in different economic systems

objectives.text: Explain decision-making in market, planned and mixed economies.
Explain how resources are allocated in these systems.
Explain the nature and meaning of a production possibility curve.
Explain the shape of the PPC: constant and increasing opportunity costs.
Explain the causes and consequences of shifts in a PPC.
Explain the significance of a position within a PPC.
Define free goods and private (economic) goods.
Define public goods.
Define merit goods and explain under-consumption through imperfect information.
Define demerit goods and explain over-consumption through imperfect information.

children.name: The price system and the microeconomy (AS Level)

objectives.text: Explain effective demand.
Distinguish individual from market demand and supply.
Identify the determinants of demand.
Identify the determinants of supply.
Explain the causes of a shift in the demand curve.
Explain the causes of a shift in the supply curve.
Distinguish a shift of a curve from a movement along it.

children.name: Price elasticity, income elasticity and cross elasticity of demand

objectives.text: Define PED, YED and XED.
State the formulae for and calculate PED, YED and XED.
Explain the significance of relative percentage changes and of the size and sign of each coefficient.
Describe elasticity values: perfectly elastic, highly elastic, unitary, highly inelastic and perfectly inelastic.
Explain how PED varies along a straight-line demand curve.
Explain the factors affecting PED, YED and XED.
Explain the relationship between PED and total expenditure on a product.
Explain the implications of PED, YED and XED for decision-making.
Define PES.
State the formula for and calculate PES.
Explain the significance of relative percentage changes and of the size and sign of the coefficient.
Explain the factors affecting PES.
Explain the implications for the speed and ease with which firms react to changed market conditions.

children.name: The interaction of demand and supply

objectives.text: Define market equilibrium and disequilibrium.
Explain the effects of shifts in demand and supply on equilibrium price and quantity.
Explain relationships between markets: joint demand, alternative demand, derived demand and joint supply.
Explain the functions of price in resource allocation: rationing, signalling and incentivising.
Explain the meaning and significance of consumer surplus.
Explain the meaning and significance of producer surplus.
Explain the causes of changes in consumer and producer surplus.
Explain how PED and PES determine the extent of these changes.

children.name: Reasons for government intervention in markets
children.description: Market failure (defined at 7.3.5-7.3.6 for A Level) is taught in the lesson covered here.

objectives.text: Explain intervention to address the non-provision of public goods.
Explain intervention to address over-consumption of demerit goods and under-consumption of merit goods.
Explain why governments control prices in markets.

children.name: Methods and effects of government intervention in markets

objectives.text: Explain the impact and incidence of specific indirect taxes.
Explain the impact and incidence of subsidies.
Explain direct provision of goods and services.
Explain maximum and minimum prices.
Explain buffer stock schemes.
Explain the provision of information.
Distinguish income as a flow from wealth as a stock.
Describe the Gini coefficient as a measure of inequality (calculation not required).
Explain the economic reasons for inequality of income and wealth.
Evaluate policies to redistribute income and wealth: minimum wage, transfer payments, progressive income taxes, inheritance and capital taxes, state provision of essential goods and services.
Explain the meaning of national income.
Explain the measurement of national income: GDP, GNI and NNI.
Explain the adjustment of measures from market prices to basic prices.
Explain the adjustment of measures from gross values to net values.

children.name: Introduction to the circular flow of income

objectives.text: Describe the circular flow of income in a closed and an open economy, including the international sector.
Explain injections and leakages (the multiplier is not required at AS).
Explain equilibrium and disequilibrium in the flow (marginal and average propensities are not required at AS).

children.name: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply analysis

objectives.text: Define aggregate demand.
Explain the components of AD: AD = C + I + G + (X - M).
Explain the determinants of AD (detailed knowledge of components is not required).
Explain the downward-sloping shape of the AD curve.
Explain the causes of a shift in the AD curve.
Define aggregate supply.
Explain the determinants of AS.
Describe the shape of SRAS and of LRAS (a vertical line, or in three sections).
Explain the causes of a shift in SRAS and in LRAS.
Distinguish a movement along from a shift in AD and AS.
Explain how equilibrium real output, the price level and employment are established in the AD/AS model.
Explain the effects of shifts in AD and AS on real output, the price level and employment.
Explain the meaning of economic growth.
Explain the measurement of economic growth.
Distinguish growth in nominal GDP from growth in real GDP.
Explain the causes of economic growth.
Explain the consequences of economic growth.
Explain the meaning of unemployment.
Explain the measures of unemployment and the difficulties of measurement.
Explain the causes and types of unemployment: frictional, structural, cyclical, seasonal and technological.
Explain the consequences of unemployment.
Define inflation, deflation and disinflation.
Explain the measurement of changes in the price level with the CPI and the difficulties of measurement.
Distinguish money (nominal) values from real data.
Explain the causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull.
Explain the consequences of inflation.
Explain the use of government policy to achieve price stability, low unemployment and economic growth (conflicts and trade-offs are not required at AS).
Explain the meaning of the government budget.
Distinguish a budget deficit from a budget surplus.
Explain the meaning and significance of the national debt.
Explain taxation: direct and indirect, progressive, regressive and proportional taxes; marginal and average tax rates; reasons for taxation.
Explain government spending: capital and current, and the reasons for it.
Distinguish expansionary from contractionary fiscal policy.
Use AD/AS analysis to show the impact of fiscal policy on national income, real output, the price level and employment.
Define monetary policy.
Explain the tools of monetary policy: interest rates, the money supply and credit regulations.
Distinguish expansionary from contractionary monetary policy.
Use AD/AS analysis to show the impact of monetary policy on national income, real output, the price level and employment.
Explain the meaning of supply-side policy in terms of its effect on LRAS.
Explain its objectives: increasing productivity and productive capacity.
Explain its tools, such as training, infrastructure and support for technological improvement.
Use AD/AS analysis to show the impact of supply-side policy on national income, real output, the price level and employment.
Distinguish absolute from comparative advantage.
Explain the benefits of specialisation and free trade, including the trading possibility curve.
Explain exports, imports and the terms of trade, including their measurement, the causes of changes and the impact of changes.
Explain the limitations of the theories of absolute and comparative advantage.
Explain the meaning of protectionism.
Explain tariffs, import quotas, export subsidies, embargoes and excessive administrative burdens, and their impact.
Evaluate the arguments for and against protectionism.

children.name: Current account of the balance of payments

objectives.text: Explain the components of the current account: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income; define balance, deficit and surplus.
Calculate the balance of trade in goods, in services, in goods and services, and the current account balance.
Explain the causes of imbalances in the current account.
Explain the consequences of imbalances for the domestic and external economy.

children.name: Exchange rates
children.description: The Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve (11.2.5) are taught in the lesson covered here.

objectives.text: Define an exchange rate.
Explain the determination of a floating exchange rate.
Distinguish depreciation from appreciation of a floating rate.
Explain the causes of changes in a floating rate: the demand for and supply of the currency.
Use AD/AS analysis to show the impact of exchange rate changes on national income, real output, the price level and employment.

children.name: Policies to correct imbalances in the current account of the balance of payments

objectives.text: Explain stability of the current account as a policy objective.
Explain the effect of fiscal, monetary, supply-side and protectionist policies on the current account.

topics.name: A Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 7-11: A Level only; examined in Papers 3 and 4 (AS content is assumed knowledge and is not the direct focus).

children.name: The price system and the microeconomy (A Level)

objectives.text: Define and calculate total utility and marginal utility.
Explain diminishing marginal utility.
Explain the equi-marginal principle.
Derive an individual demand curve.
Evaluate marginal utility theory and its assumption of rational behaviour.
Explain an indifference curve and a budget line.
Explain the causes of a shift in the budget line.
Explain income, substitution and price effects for normal, inferior and Giffen goods.
Evaluate the model of indifference curves.

children.name: Efficiency and market failure
children.description: Market failure (7.3.5-7.3.6) is taught in the lesson covered at 3.1.

objectives.text: Define productive efficiency and allocative efficiency.
Explain the conditions for productive and allocative efficiency.
Explain Pareto optimality.
Define dynamic efficiency.
Define market failure.
Explain the reasons for market failure.

children.name: Private costs and benefits, externalities and social costs and benefits

objectives.text: Define and calculate social cost as private plus external cost, including the marginal versions.
Define and calculate social benefit as private plus external benefit, including the marginal versions.
Define positive and negative externalities.
Explain positive and negative externalities of consumption and production.
Explain the deadweight welfare losses arising from positive and negative externalities.
Explain asymmetric information and moral hazard.
Use costs and benefits to analyse decisions (net present value is not required).

children.name: Types of cost, revenue and profit, short-run and long-run production

objectives.text: Explain the short-run production function: fixed and variable factors, total, average and marginal product, and diminishing returns.
Define and calculate fixed, variable, total, average and marginal costs and explain the shape of the short-run cost curves.
Explain the long-run production function: no fixed factors, and returns to scale.
Explain the shape of the long-run average cost curve and the minimum efficient scale.
Explain the relationship between economies of scale and decreasing average costs.
Explain internal and external economies of scale.
Explain internal and external diseconomies of scale.
Define and calculate total, average and marginal revenue.
Define normal, subnormal and supernormal profit.
Calculate supernormal and subnormal profit.

children.name: Different market structures
children.description: Cartels (7.7.4) are taught in the collusion lesson covered here.

objectives.text: Distinguish perfect competition from imperfect competition: monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and natural monopoly.
Describe each market by the number of buyers and sellers, product differentiation, freedom of entry and availability of information.
Explain legal, market, cost and physical barriers to entry and exit.
Explain the performance of firms in each structure: revenue curves, short- and long-run output and profit, shutdown price and the supply curve under perfect competition.
Explain efficiency and X-inefficiency, contestable markets, price and non-price competition, collusion and the Prisoner's Dilemma with a two-player pay-off matrix.
Define and calculate the concentration ratio.
Explain the reasons for different sizes of firm.
Explain internal growth: organic growth and diversification.
Explain external growth by horizontal, vertical and conglomerate integration: methods, reasons and consequences.
Explain cartels: the conditions for an effective cartel and its consequences.
Explain the principal-agent problem arising from differing objectives of owners and managers.

children.name: Differing objectives and policies of firms
children.description: The principal-agent problem (7.7.5) is taught in the objectives lesson covered here.

objectives.text: Explain the traditional profit-maximising objective.
Explain other objectives: survival, profit satisficing, sales maximisation and revenue maximisation.
Explain first-, second- and third-degree price discrimination, the conditions for it and its consequences.
Explain other pricing policies: limit pricing, predatory pricing and price leadership.
Explain the relationship between PED and a firm's revenue, for a normal and a kinked demand curve.

children.name: Government policies to achieve efficient resource allocation and correct market failure

objectives.text: Apply and assess measures to tackle market failure: specific and ad valorem taxes, subsidies, price controls, production quotas, prohibitions and licences, regulation and deregulation, direct provision, pollution permits, property rights, nationalisation and privatisation, provision of information, and behavioural insights and 'nudge' theory.
Define government failure and explain its causes and consequences in microeconomic intervention.

children.name: Equity and redistribution of income and wealth

objectives.text: Distinguish equity from equality.
Distinguish equity from efficiency.
Distinguish absolute from relative poverty.
Explain the poverty trap.
Evaluate policies towards equity and equality: negative income tax, universal and means-tested benefits, universal basic income.

children.name: Labour market forces and government intervention

objectives.text: Explain the demand for labour as a derived demand.
Explain the factors affecting the demand for labour in a firm or an occupation.
Explain shifts in and movements along the demand curve for labour.
Define and calculate marginal revenue product and derive a firm's demand for labour from it.
Explain the wage and non-wage factors affecting the supply of labour.
Explain shifts in and movements along the supply curve of labour.
Explain wage determination in perfect markets: equilibrium wage and employment.
Explain wage determination in imperfect markets: trade unions, a national minimum wage and monopsony.
Explain how labour market forces determine wage differentials.
Define transfer earnings and economic rent and explain the factors affecting them.
Define the multiplier and state the formulae for it in a closed and open economy, with and without a government sector.
Calculate the propensities to save, consume and import and the rates of tax (average and marginal).
Use the multiplier to calculate the effect of a change in AD on national income.
Explain the components of AD and their determinants: consumption and savings functions, autonomous and induced investment, the accelerator, government spending and net exports.
Explain the full employment and equilibrium levels of national income, and inflationary and deflationary gaps.
Distinguish actual from potential growth.
Explain positive and negative output gaps.
Explain the business cycle: phases, causes and automatic stabilisers.
Evaluate policies to promote economic growth.
Explain inclusive economic growth, its effect on equity and equality, and policies to promote it.
Explain sustainable economic growth, resource use and conservation, the effects of growth on the environment and climate change, and policies to mitigate them.
Define full employment.
Explain equilibrium and disequilibrium unemployment, including hysteresis.
Distinguish voluntary from involuntary unemployment.
Define the natural rate of unemployment and explain its determinants and policy implications.
Describe patterns and trends in employment and unemployment.
Explain geographical and occupational mobility of labour and the factors affecting it.
Evaluate policies to reduce unemployment.

children.name: Money and banking
children.description: Policies to reduce inflation (9.4.6) are taught in the inflation lesson covered at 4.6.

objectives.text: Define money and explain its functions and characteristics.
Define the money supply.
Explain the quantity theory of money (MV = PT).
Explain the functions and objectives of commercial banks: deposits, lending, balance sheet items, reserve and capital ratios, liquidity, security and profitability.

Explain the causes of changes in the money supply in an open economy: credit creation and the bank credit multiplier, the central bank, deficit financing, quantitative easing and the balance of payments.
Evaluate policies to reduce inflation.
Explain the demand for money using liquidity preference theory.
Explain interest rate determination using the loanable funds and Keynesian theories.

children.name: Government macroeconomic policy objectives
children.description: Objectives in terms of inflation, the balance of payments, unemployment, growth, development, sustainability and redistribution (10.1.1) are taught in the policy-objectives lesson covered at 5.1.

objectives.text: Explain macroeconomic objectives for inflation, the balance of payments, unemployment, growth, development, sustainability and the redistribution of income and wealth.

children.name: Links between macroeconomic problems and their interrelatedness

objectives.text: Explain the relationship between the internal and the external value of money.
Explain the relationship between the balance of payments and inflation.
Explain the relationship between growth and inflation.
Explain the relationship between growth and the balance of payments.
Explain the relationship between inflation and unemployment: the traditional and the expectations-augmented (short- and long-run) Phillips curves.

children.name: Effectiveness of policy options to meet all macroeconomic objectives

objectives.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of fiscal (including the Laffer curve), monetary, supply-side (market-based and interventionist), exchange rate and international trade policies against the different objectives.
Explain problems and conflicts arising from the outcomes of these policies.
Explain government failure in macroeconomic policies.

children.name: Policies to correct disequilibrium in the balance of payments
children.description: The effects of policies (11.1.2) and expenditure-switching against expenditure-reducing policies (11.1.3) are taught in the lesson covered at 6.5.

objectives.text: Explain the components of the balance of payments accounts: current account, financial account and capital account.
Explain the effect of fiscal, monetary, supply-side, protectionist and exchange rate policies on the balance of payments.
Distinguish expenditure-switching from expenditure-reducing policies.

children.name: Exchange rates at A Level
children.description: The effects of exchange rate changes, including Marshall-Lerner and the J-curve (11.2.5), are taught in the lesson covered at 6.4.

objectives.text: Distinguish nominal from real exchange rates and explain trade-weighted exchange rates.
Explain the determination of exchange rates under fixed and managed systems.
Distinguish revaluation from devaluation of a fixed exchange rate.
Explain changes in the exchange rate under different exchange rate systems.
Explain the effects of changing exchange rates on the external economy using Marshall-Lerner and J-curve analysis.
Classify economies by level of development.
Classify economies by level of national income.

Evaluate indicators of living standards and development: real per capita national income, purchasing power parity, issues of comparison, non-monetary indicators, composite indicators (HDI, MEW, MPI) and the Kuznets curve.
Compare economic growth rates and living standards over time and between countries.

children.name: Characteristics of countries at different levels of development

objectives.text: Explain population growth and structure: birth rate, death rate, infant mortality, net migration, optimum population and urbanisation.
Calculate the Gini coefficient and use Lorenz curve analysis of income distribution.
Explain economic structure: employment composition by sector and the pattern of trade at different levels of development.

children.name: Relationship between countries at different levels of development

objectives.text: Explain international aid: forms, reasons for giving, effects and importance.
Explain trade and investment between countries at different levels of development.
Define multinational companies and explain their activities and consequences.
Define foreign direct investment and explain its consequences.
Explain the causes and consequences of external debt.
Explain the role of the International Monetary Fund.
Explain the role of the World Bank.
Explain the meaning of globalisation and its causes and consequences.
Distinguish a free trade area, a customs union, a monetary union and a full economic union.
Explain trade creation and trade diversion.

topics.name: Examination skills
topics.description: Not a content section of the syllabus: our grouping of the assessment objectives (AO1 knowledge and understanding, AO2 analysis, AO3 evaluation), the command words and the structure of the data-response and essay papers.

children.name: Data response: diagrams, data and calculations
Using source material, diagrams and calculations

objectives.text: Select, interpret and organise economic information in written, numerical and diagrammatic form.
Use clearly labelled diagrams and calculations to support an answer.
Recognise assumptions and limitations of economic information and models, and assess the strengths and weaknesses of arguments.
Communicate reasoned judgements and conclusions, recognising that some decisions involve priorities and value judgements.
